message.content:
Lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) are both placental mammals, but they belong to different orders—Carnivora for the lion and Perissodactyla for the zebra.  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of the clade **Laurasiatheria**, which includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla. This ancestor lived roughly 90–100 million years ago during the late Cretaceous/early Paleogene period, before the diversification of the modern orders. In other words, the common ancestor was a small, insectivorous‑to‑herbivorous mammal that gave rise to the diverse lineages that eventually led to lions and zebras.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) are both mammals, but belong to different orders: lions are Carnivora, zebras are Perissodactyla. Their common ancestor would be at the level of the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, or maybe earlier. But we can give a more precise answer: The last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). That ancestor lived around 100 million years ago. So answer: The last common ancestor of all placental mammals, likely a small, insectivorous mammal that lived ~100 million years ago. Or we could mention the ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria. Actually, Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria is older than that of all placental mammals. But the question might be answered as: The last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, which existed about 90-100 million years ago. So answer accordingly.
